direct_answer: Bunions and big-toe arthritis can make shoes painful and walking less steady. Wide, deep, supportive shoes, padding and podiatry help many people. Surgery is an option for some, but recovery needs careful planning in frailty.

content:
A bunion is a bony lump at the side of the big toe joint. Bunions and arthritis of the big toe joint are common in later life and can make finding comfortable shoes hard.

This guide explains practical options for bunions with arthritis and frailty. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or treatment plan.

How bunions affect daily life

  • Pressure and rubbing from shoes.
  • Pain and stiffness when pushing off to walk.
  • Wearing loose slippers because shoes hurt, which can raise falls risk.
  • Walking less because of pain.

Choosing shoes

  • Look for wide and deep toe boxes and soft uppers.
  • Choose adjustable fastenings, such as Velcro or laces.
  • Pick a firm, low heel and a grippy sole.
  • Have your feet measured, as size and width can change with age.

Other things that may help

  • Bunion pads or toe spacers to reduce rubbing.
  • Insoles or orthoses from a podiatrist.
  • Painkillers or gels, discussed with a pharmacist or GP.
  • Keeping active with supportive footwear.

Surgery

Surgery may be considered if pain persists despite these measures. For older or frail people, the decision includes recovery time, reduced weight-bearing and help needed at home. Discuss the benefits and risks with your GP and surgeon.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will a bunion get worse?

Bunions often slowly get worse, but symptoms can be managed with footwear and care.

Should I wear slippers all day?

Backless slippers can increase falls risk. Supportive, fastened footwear is safer.

Can I see a podiatrist on the NHS?

Ask your GP, as access varies by area.
